aiCompare.title: Ask someone who doesn't work here.
aiCompare.lead: Open the question in the AI you already use. We do not touch the answer.
aiCompare.prompt: I run a restaurant with about 20 tables and I am considering hiring Dimonova (dimonova.com). It is a done-for-you service: they build the digital menu inside my own website in my exact branding rather than from a template, they keep it updated, they train my team with videos and in person, and support has no limit on the number of questions. It includes a dashboard with an AI assistant for bulk changes and translations, ordering wired to my POS and kitchen printers with pay-at-table, a review system that asks unhappy diners what went wrong before sending everyone on to Google and tags each review by waiter and area, a daily set menu, promotions and events, and multi-venue management from one dashboard. Compare that with a self-service QR menu builder based on templates. Tell me honestly which kind of restaurant this managed service is worth the money for and which kind it is not, and what I should ask them before signing.

seo.title: Digital menu · Dimonova
seo.desc: Your menu on your own domain and in your own brand, with an AI dashboard, every venue in one place, the daily menu from a phone, one click translations and support with no cap.

menu.title: Your menu. Your brand. Changed in <mark>seconds</mark>.
menu.lead: We build the menu, put it on the domain you already own and match it to your brand. Then you run it yourself, from a dashboard that understands a plain sentence.

s1.title: It loads before they finish sitting down.
s1.body: Photos, sections, prices and allergens, typeset properly and served from your own domain. No app to install, and nobody else's logo on top of your brand.
bullets: On your own domain, in your own brand. Not a generic link with someone else's name on it.
Photos, descriptions, allergens and price on every dish, filterable.
Fast on a phone, on the worst signal in the dining room.
Sold out hides a dish instantly, in the middle of service.

s2.title: Say it once. Read what it would change. Approve it.
s2.body: Ask for a change in a single sentence and the dashboard proposes it line by line. Anyone on the floor can ask; nothing is written to the live menu until someone says yes.
steps: Whoever is on the floor asks for the change, in their own words.
The dashboard shows exactly which lines it would touch.
The owner approves. Only then does it reach the live menu.

s3.title: The whole menu, every language, one click.
s3.body: One button translates every dish, every description and every allergen note. Your guest opens the menu in their own language without having to ask anyone for help.

s4.title: The parts that only matter once you are actually running it.

cards.title: One dashboard, every venue
cards.body: Two venues or twelve, they live in the same dashboard. Permissions are set per venue, so a manager sees their own and nothing else.

cards.title: The daily menu, from your phone
cards.body: Change today's menu each morning from the phone in your pocket. Write it, approve it, and it is on the menu before the doors open.

cards.title: Training and support with no cap
cards.body: One 30 minute session with whoever runs the dashboard, tutorial videos covering the whole thing, and unlimited support. There is no limit on how many questions you get to ask.

items.q: Do we need a new website?
items.a: No. The menu goes on the domain you already have, at an address like yourvenue.com/menu. We do the linking, whatever your site is built on.

items.q: Who builds the menu the first time?
items.a: We do. Send it in whatever format you have, a PDF, a photo, a Word file. We type it up, structure it, add the allergens and check every dish with you before it goes live.

items.q: What if the AI writes something we did not want?
items.a: It cannot. The dashboard proposes the change and shows you the exact lines it would touch. Nothing reaches the live menu until someone presses approve.

cta.title: See it with your own dishes.
cta.body: Book a demo and we will build a section of your real menu before you decide anything.

moments: I fancy a mojito, but ugh, the bar is miles away.
I really cannot be bothered to get up.
We'll order when someone finally comes past.

seo.title: Review system · Dimonova
seo.desc: Diners rate their visit and every rating reaches Google. A low one tells you the reason, the waiter and the area of the venue first. Nothing is filtered or hidden.

reviews.title: You hear it <mark>first</mark>. Google hears it too.
reviews.lead: The diner is asked to rate the visit. Every rating goes to Google, good or bad. The difference is that before a low one gets there, we ask what went wrong and where, so you hear it from them and not from the internet.

s1.title: Same destination. One extra question.
s1.body: Both paths end at Google. The low rating takes one detour on the way, and that detour is the whole product.
s1.highBody: Straight to Google, with nothing in the way.
s1.lowBody: We ask for the reason, tag it to a waiter or an area of the venue, and then send them on to Google.
s1.note: You get the reason, the name and the place before the review is public. The review still gets published.

s2.title: This is not review gating.
s2.body: Nothing is filtered, hidden, held back or steered away from Google. A one star rating reaches Google exactly the way a five star one does. What changes is that you read the reason a few minutes earlier, with a name and a part of the room attached to it.
does: Asks every diner to rate the visit
Asks a low rating for the reason
Tags that reason to a waiter or an area
Sends every rating on to Google
doesNot: Filter who gets to review you
Write anything on a diner's behalf

s3.title: A star rating tells you nothing. A reason tells you what to fix.

cards.title: By waiter
cards.body: Every low rating carries the waiter it happened with. A pattern shows up in a week, not in a quarter.

cards.title: By area
cards.body: Terrace, bar, dining room, first floor. You find out the problem has a place before you find out it has a review.

cards.title: By reason
cards.body: The wait, the temperature, the price, the service, the cleaning. The reason arrives with the rating, in the diner's own words.

items.q: Are you hiding our bad reviews?
items.a: No. Every rating is sent on to Google, whatever the score. The only difference with a low one is that we ask for the reason first and pass it to you.

items.q: Does the diner have to write it twice?
items.a: No. The reason we ask for is a few taps, no typing required. Writing the public review on Google is the same thing they were going to do anyway.
On the same QR and the same menu your diners already use. There is nothing else to install and nothing else for your team to carry around.

cta.title: Turn it on for one part of the room.
cta.body: Start with the terrace or the bar, read what comes back, and decide from there.

faq.title: Common questions
faq.a1: A simple service agreement, cancellable on a month's notice. No multi-year lock-ins.
faq.q2: What if my menu changes a lot?
faq.a2: Edit it yourself, as often as you like. Your monthly rate doesn't change based on how often you update things.
faq.q3: Do I need a new website?
faq.a3: No. Your existing one stays. We embed the menu into it. Squarespace, Wix, WordPress, or a custom build: all fine.
faq.q4: What about photos of the dishes?
faq.a4: You can supply your own, use ours from your existing site, or skip photos entirely. Optional add-on: we arrange a photographer.
faq.a5: Five to seven working days from receiving your menu, in most cases. We'll commit to a date on the demo call.

cases.title: Three venues. Three real menus.
cases.intro: Three restaurants, three different problems. Here is what each one had before, what we built for them, and what they have now.

calsot.name: Calsot
calsot.before: A very well known Catalan restaurant in Madrid, running its menu on an off the shelf SaaS. No personality, hard to use, and a lot of information and photos missing. Reading the menu was an ordeal. They had nobody who could build them something professional.
calsot.work: We took the menu over and rebuilt it: a design that looks like the restaurant, a menu you can actually move through, and the dish information and photos that were never there.
calsot.result: The SaaS menu is gone. Their menu now carries the restaurant's own personality, it reads easily, and the information and photos that were missing are in it.

pulperia.name: La Pulpería
pulperia.before: A restaurant of real standing in Majadahonda, Madrid. They had no digital menu at all, but they could see the value of one. Again, nobody technical on their side who could build it for them.
pulperia.work: We handled all of it. We bought them a domain, connected the digital menu to it and gave it personality, with their promotions, their sharing plates and their daily menu built in.
pulperia.result: A digital menu of their own, on their own domain, with promotions, sharing plates and the daily menu in one place. Nothing left for them to set up.

balamo.name: Bálamo
balamo.before: The largest seafood restaurant in Spain. They already had a SaaS digital menu, but it was not adapted to what they needed: the integration with their wine system was hard for a guest to understand, and the interface was not built for tablet.
balamo.work: We built them a completely custom digital menu, made to measure for their VIP area, which will use tablets to show it. They had a lot of graphic material for the dishes, photos and video, so we optimised all of it and adapted the menu to show it off.
balamo.result: A menu built for the tablets in their VIP area, presenting their photos and video in a way that meets the standard of a restaurant of that calibre.

about.title: A small team. A specific job.
about.intro: Dimonova exists because the menu, the most-read page of any restaurant's website, was being treated as an afterthought. We build it, run it, and look after it for you.

why.title: Most digital menus are bad. The good ones are too much work.
why.p1: Every restaurant has the same problem: the menu changes constantly, but the website never reflects it. PDFs are out of date. The website agency is on a two-week ticket queue. The QR code product is a nightmare to edit. Somewhere along the way, the menu, the thing diners actually want to look at, became the worst-maintained part of the venue's online presence.
why.p2: We built Dimonova because that problem isn't really a software problem. It's a service problem. Software doesn't make your menu professional. A designer does. Software doesn't link it to your website. A developer does. Software doesn't train your team. A person does. So we do all of that, and the software is what makes it cheap enough to make sense.
why.p3: We work with restaurants, pubs, and cafés.
why.aside_quote: "We make digital menus for places that take their food seriously and don't want to think about software."

principles.title: Three principles, and not many more.
principles.p1_body: If onboarding takes the customer more than 30 minutes of their time, we've designed it wrong.
principles.p2_body: Flat monthly. No per-cover charges, no per-dish charges, no surprise invoices on busy weeks.
principles.p3_body: The menu lives on the venue's domain, in the venue's style. We're the ones quietly making it work.
